note: AGENT-SPEC section 5. The single source of truth for the agent's tool surface: src/agent/tools.ts imports this file and src-tauri/src/agent_mcp.rs include_str!s it, so every provider and the MCP server present byte-identical schemas. Anthropic caches the tools+system prefix, so any edit here is a cache-invalidating change: bump version and re-baseline (EVAL.md section 4). B3 added `canvasTools`, offered only to a run with a canvas target (AGENT-SPEC section 5, canvas-agent-spec section 1.3): `tools` did not move one byte, so no baseline row moves and no gated run sees a different prefix. Every schema is self-contained, with no $ref and no $defs: each adapter puts `parameters` on the wire alone (openai.ts renderTools, anthropic.ts input_schema, agent_mcp.rs parse_tools), so a $defs sibling of `tools` would never reach the model and a pointer into it would not resolve. The block union is written out in both tools that take one, and tools.test.ts pins the two copies equal. C2 added `at` and `span` to both arms of that union, optional and clamped rather than required and refused (canvas-grid-spec 2.6): `tools` still did not move one byte, and canvas-place.test.ts pins that too.

tools.name: list_tables
tools.description: List every table in the database: name, approximate row count, and the table comment when it has one. Call this first when you do not know which tables exist.

tools.name: describe_tables
tools.description: Definitions of several tables at once: columns with types, primary and foreign keys, column comments, and real sample values for low-cardinality columns. Ask for every table you might need in ONE call; do not call this once per table. An unknown name comes back as an error listing the valid names.

names.description: Table names, exactly as list_tables spelled them.

tools.name: peek_values
tools.description: Distinct real values stored in one column. Use this before filtering on any text, enum, or status column, so the filter matches the exact stored spelling and case. The reply marks whether more values exist than were shown; on a very large table the values are a sample and the reply says so.

table.description: Table name, exactly as list_tables spelled it.

limit.description: How many distinct values to return, 1 to 50.

tools.name: run_sql
tools.description: Execute ONE read-only PostgreSQL statement (SELECT, WITH ... SELECT, or EXPLAIN) and return its rows. Anything that writes, locks rows, or bundles more than one statement is refused. Errors come back as text starting with ERROR:, so read it, fix the query, and run it again.

sql.description: One PostgreSQL statement and nothing else: never prose, never a markdown fence, no trailing semicolon needed.

tools.name: probe
tools.description: Run up to 6 small read-only checks in one call, 5 rows each, to verify an assumption before you trust a final query: min and max of a timestamp you filter on, a count of rows outside the expected order, a distinct list. Same rules as run_sql; each query is reported separately, and one failure does not stop the rest.

canvasTools.name: canvas_write
canvasTools.description: Append blocks to the canvas the user is reading. A `result` block carries one read-only SELECT: this tool runs it, keeps up to 200 rows on the canvas with their columns, and opens it on the face its rows deserve. A `note` block carries markdown you write. The reply gives every block a short id, and every result its columns and first 5 rows, so the note you write last describes what actually came back.

text.description: Markdown. One bold lead-in ending in a colon and two to four bullets read well, each bullet ONE finding with its own figure. Never a markdown table: the result blocks carry the rows.

at.description: Where this block stands, in grid cells counted from the canvas's top left, as canvas_read prints them. Omit it and the canvas finds the first free place in reading order.

span.description: How many cells wide and tall this block is. Omit it and the canvas gives this kind its own size: a note small, a chart larger, a table larger still. A span wider than the canvas has columns is narrowed to fit and the reply says so.

sql.description: One read-only PostgreSQL statement and nothing else, under the same rules as run_sql: never prose, never a markdown fence.

title.description: At most six words naming what this block shows, identifiers in backticks. Leave it off the first block of an answer: that one wears the question.

note.description: One sentence above the face saying what the number means. Most results in an analysis carry none, because the note block holds the reading.

face.description: Which face the block opens on. Omit it and the canvas picks: the chart when the rows make one, the values when there is one row, the table otherwise.

at.description: Where this block stands, in grid cells counted from the canvas's top left, as canvas_read prints them. Omit it and the canvas finds the first free place in reading order.

span.description: How many cells wide and tall this block is. Omit it and the canvas gives this kind its own size: a note small, a chart larger, a table larger still. A span wider than the canvas has columns is narrowed to fit and the reply says so.

after.description: Put them after this block instead of at the end of the canvas: the id, or its first 4 characters, as canvas_read printed it.

canvasTools.name: canvas_replace
canvasTools.description: Replace one block of the canvas, keeping its place. Use it when new work supersedes a block you wrote rather than writing a second one beside it; a result block's statement is run again. A block you did not write belongs to the user and is refused, and no block can be emptied: deleting is the user's own action.

block_id.description: The id, or its first 4 characters, as canvas_read printed it.

canvasTools.name: canvas_read
canvasTools.description: What the canvas already holds: how many columns wide it is, then every block's id, kind, first line and place on the grid, and for a result its columns, its row count and the face it is on. Call it before writing into a canvas that is not empty, so you add to the document instead of repeating it, and before placing a block yourself, so `at` and `span` are written against the grid that is really there.
